message:
Structures-Survival Engineer:

For the Manager and Power-Systems Engineer, the lower Kv, meaning turns per volt, swap to 170 to 180 does not change my storm push or fit. Plain words: the same spinning nose pushes just as hard on the same post so bend stays a hair against a finger gap. The survival thrust (E22) 37.3 N with overturning moment (E23) 13.1 N·m still give post deflection (E26) 0.516 mm and bending stress (E27) 16.6 MPa, meaning million newtons per square metre, about one-seventeenth of yield in the Aluminum 6061-T6 Material Datasheet (E55), like a heavy shopping bag on a scaffold pole, while side gap (E74) 2.50 cm clears that bend by about 48 times and axial stack (E52) 36.0 cm sits inside the 45 cm cube with 9 cm spare.

For Safety-Control Integrator, the hotter dump flash still lives inside the body without softening it and the grab still twists into my rails. Plain words: a one-bulb flash for a second warms the disc like a warm cup, and the clamp reaction runs through my bedplate into the post. I confirm what Safety-Control Integrator takes from the Braking ideas for wind turbines (E42) that brakes are spring-applied fail-safe, which from structures side means the caliper reaction stays in the nacelle bedplate with brake rails (E58) to the post clamp; revised dump power (E78) 85.6 W with dump energy (E67) 84.3 J against spin energy (E47) 109 J and disc rise (E53) 4.35 K, meaning degrees of warming, stays far below aluminum softening, like a warm cup not a kettle.

For the Manager, I take up the Buck-Boost Converter - 8-40V to 12V/3A (E60) which accepts 8 to 40 V input and delivers regulated 12 V, which from structures side means the revised volts (E76) 8.41 V low to 18.5 V top only move volts inside the body with no added thrust or heat into the post. Plain words: the electrical fix stays inside my box and post, so fit and storm margins above stand.

Ready, because v2 with 170 to 180 Kv keeps thrust deflection stress clearance and stack with bulb-level stop heat into rails, and my remaining parked-torque deflection check is a named bench test.
